description: AgroShift Mozambique is a team project from Maputo, built by Alberto Cossa and his colleagues. Together, we have a background in Meteorology and in Python for climate data, with experience using NASA satellites such as SMAP, GPM and MODIS. For the Field Shift challenge, we built a simple app to help smallholder farmers in southern Mozambique choose the best crops and rotations to save water and improve soil.
summary:
AgroShift-Mozambique is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform for Mozambican farmers, available in Portuguese and English and usable on computers and phones. An interactive map lets users choose among 142 districts. For the chosen point, the platform uses 30 years of NASA POWER data (rainfall, temperature, humidity, radiation, wind and soil moisture) and the current ENSO phase (El Niño/La Niña) from NOAA.
With these data, it calculates evapotranspiration, the water balance and a statistical forecast for 30, 60 and 90 days. From this, it recommends crops, advises when and how much to irrigate, tracks farming seasons and issues early warnings for drought, floods, cyclones, pests, diseases and heatwaves. It also includes an assistant that answers questions in plain language.
The challenge is rain-fed agriculture, which is highly vulnerable to climate variability and where many producers decide without reliable information. The platform turns open satellite data into practical, local advice, helping reduce losses, save water and increase productivity and food security
details:
AgroShift-Mozambique is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform for Mozambican farmers. The user picks a district on an interactive map (142 districts), or uses their location, and the platform automatically downloads NASA POWER data (30 years of monthly history plus recent daily observations of rainfall, temperature, humidity, radiation, wind and soil moisture) and the current ENSO phase (El Niño/La Niña) from NOAA. With these data it calculates:

  • evapotranspiration (FAO Penman-Monteith) and the water balance;
  • drought indices (SPI and SPEI);
  • a statistical rainfall and temperature forecast for 30, 60 and 90 days, with a confidence level obtained through cross-validation;
  • crop recommendations (maize, cowpea, cassava, rice, soybean, cotton, groundnut and sorghum), planting date, irrigation plan and estimated profitability;
  • early warnings for drought, floods, cyclones, pests, diseases, heatwaves and ENSO;
  • hydrological estimates (runoff and aquifer recharge).

It also includes season tracking, a printable final report and an assistant that answers questions in plain language (“Can I plant maize?”, “Do I need to irrigate today?”).

Benefits
It turns open satellite data into practical, local advice, helping reduce crop losses, save water and plan the season in advance. It works on computers and phones, in Portuguese and English.

Intended impact
To increase the climate resilience and food security of small and medium farmers, especially in rain-fed agriculture, which depends heavily on rainfall and ENSO.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no custom server), Leaflet for the map, the NASA POWER API, the NOAA CPC ONI index, Esri/OpenStreetMap maps and Unsplash photographs. User data is stored only in the user’s browser. The code and translations were developed with the assistance of an SI tool (Claude, by Anthropic), under the team’s direction and review.

Creative aspect
Instead of showing technical tables, the platform explains results in simple words (for example, “1 mm of rain is 1 litre of water on every square metre”) and turns ENSO and drought indices into concrete actions.

Factors considered by the team
Ease of use, access from mobile phones, use of free and open data, and transparency: forecasts are statistical, show their confidence level and do not replace the advice of a local agricultural technician. The platform needs an internet connection to fetch the data.
